newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel rejects Clinton jab on settlements.
newsitem.headline: Israel rejects Clinton jab on settlements.

text.p: Israel on Tuesday rejected criticism by U.S. President Bill Clinton on Jewish settlements and vowed to strengthen its hold on the outposts that Clinton called an obstacle to peace.

At the White House on Monday, Clinton toughened his stance against an Israeli settlement revival in occupied Arab lands by right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who came to power six months ago.

"The policy of this government is to strengthen settlement in places where it exists," Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai told reporters in the Gaza Strip after visiting Jewish settlers there.

"There are natural needs and necessary growth and I believe this policy is clear and was explained to every national or international element," he said. "If there are disagreements it's better for us to talk about them."

Clinton on Monday embraced the tough language of his predecessor George Bush on the issue. Asked at the White House if he would call settlements an obstacle to peace, Clinton told reporters: "Absolutely".

Israeli-Palestinian tensions flared in the last week over Israel's decision to grant financial benefits to West Bank settlements. The cabinet action followed the killing of a settler mother and her son by Arab gunmen.
Netanyahu, now Likud leader, declined comment on Clinton's remarks when asked by reporters. But his communications chief David Bar-Illan shrugged off the U.S. presidential jab.
Bar-Illan said that Washington not Israel had to change its policy and insisted the Jewish state's relations with its close U.S. ally were as excellent as ever.

"The position of the administration on the settlements has been consistent...They are opposed to any activity on the settlements and we have to try to change their minds but obviously we haven't been able to," Bar-Illan told Reuters.

Bar-Illan voiced astonishment at reaction to the Israeli decision which he said was meant to eliminate discrimination against West Bank settlers by giving them benefits enjoyed by Israelis in other areas captured in the 1967 Middle East war.

A White House spokesman said Washington found the latest policy on settlements "a complicating factor" in peace efforts which have been stuck on the long-overdue handover of 80 percent of the West Bank town of Hebron to Palestinian rule.
A leading Palestinian, hailing Clinton's remarks, said Washington had begun playing an important role in peacemaking.

"We salute this initiative...President Clinton has realised that settlement activity is fatal to the peace process and has thus warned against it," Ahmed Korei, speaker of the 89-member Palestinian legislature, told Reuters.

Israel's relations with Washington reached a 35-year low in the early 1990s over a settlement boom spearheaded by right-wing Likud party prime minister Yitzhak Shamir and his hawkish housing minister Ariel Sharon.
President Bush held up $10 billion in U.S. loan guarantees over the settlement issue, awarding them only after Yitzhak Rabin ousted Shamir and Likud in 1993 and froze new settlement building.

Rabin, a Nobel peace laureate, was assassinated in November 1995. Netanyahu lifted the freeze after winning election in May this year. About 130,000 Jews live in the settlements scattered among two million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.
